en: If falcon-like Kalcha
Is truly keen and bold,
Then he will heed these words.
Old Kalcha will surely give
The great idol he worships.”
If you are willing, give the idol
To Semetey.
To the silver-eyed, sun-eyed,
Thunderous champion,
Say, “Here, Kalcha has given it.”
Let me take him as a gift,
And bring the gray wolf Semetey
Before you.
Agree to what he says,
And without quarrel or strife,
Lead him safely to the Khagan.
Pay the blood-price
For his lion father Manas, then return.
All the people have gathered;
We have come to face our reckoning.
After so many Chinese were slaughtered,
We have come to this pass.
Know that this is what I counsel;
Uncle Kalcha, heed my words.
Remain here and guard Beijing;
Make peace with the champion Semetey.
Negotiate without wrangling,
Do not quarrel and fight;
Return as a people reconciled.
Yesterday there was clamorous uproar,
And we began this grievous ordeal.
What horn of plenty ever sprang
From the hollow of Kaspan-Too,
From the banks of the Kara-Suu,
From the slopes of Kyr-Kayıng,
Or from the edge of Kyl-Irtysh?
We tore at one another’s beards and hair,
Fired guns and loosed arrows,
And fought in bloody struggle—
What benefit ever came of it?
From battle, turmoil, and war,
From this wretched business, when you look,
Tell me, Uncle Kongurbay,
Was your treasury filled?
Battle came and the people died;
Many different nations died.
The desolate land found no peace;
At the very word that battle was coming,
The people wailed and cried aloud.
Without quarreling or attacking,
Agree to these words;
My princely elder, pay the blood-price for Manas!
Now that your hair is gray with age,
Go safely to the Khagan;
My lord and uncle Kongurbay,
Return safely to Beijing.
That bloodthirsty champion and lion
Filled the Kara-Suu with blood,
Set the grassy lands ablaze,
And burned the valley.
He burned the valley and turned it to grease;
When his wrath was roused,
He even laid low his own father, Khan Jakyp.
That great gray wolf of violent birth,
After turning his back on the Kyrgyz,
After embracing the Chinese faith,
Speak words of conciliation to him.
Stand face-to-face,
Pour out spirits and serve food,
And offer them to one another.
Exchange words of reconciliation;
Meet and speak at length,
Bring your hearts together as one,
And return as friends.
At Karkyra, where men circle together,
Gather round and confer;
At Karkyra, where hosts assemble,
Hold council together.
Lay the matter before you,
And cast aside every grudge;
Lay your words before you,
And cast aside every wrong.
Make true peace and return.
Bid each other, ‘Farewell, and remain safe!’
Make peace once and return;
Like flour from white wheat,
Blend together, you two lions;
Like hairs from a white antelope,
You two lions who have pulled apart!
Like a great river flowing through the valley,
Become a single spring;
Move toward friendship
And remain close companions.
My lion-uncle Kongurbay,
Consent to the words I have spoken,
And grant me the idol’s power.
I made their elders bow in reverence;
I converted them wholly to the faith—
All the Buruts.”
When Külchoro had spoken thus,
Alööke’s Kongurbay said:
“Ah, they call you a heroic warrior,
And what you have said is wise.
As for that great inscribed, hollow-bellied idol—
Oh, my child, take not merely its power but its head!
If it will bring prosperity to that bloodthirsty hero,
Take not merely its power but its head.
To Manas’s only son,
As the foremost of gifts,
Present it freely.
If that idol is too small a gift,
Let him take Ezkara’s great war drum
As a magnificent offering!
Let us unite and meet face-to-face,
Eating meat from a single dish;
Let us abandon our grudges and meet,
Like a pale star in the heavens,
Chest to chest as friends.
Let us begin our roaring conversation,
And, my son, cast our thunderous valor
Into the water and leave it there.
I shall agree to what he says.
For his father, the gray wolf Manas,
I shall pay the blood-price a full thousandfold.
Bring me your prince,
Your renowned bloodthirsty lord.
Lead here the infidel eager for battle—
The blood-drinking, bloodthirsty warrior.
As blood-price for his father Manas,
My gray horses with fetlocked legs—
All are peerless thoroughbreds.
From the unbroken herds
I shall drive out and give droves of every kind,
Without even unrolling
Such a tally, I shall give livestock.
One kind of horse is dun,
With a white blaze like an amulet;
All are peerless thoroughbreds.
I shall give a drove of kulans,
All evenly matched dappled thoroughbreds;
Of these I shall give a drove.
Black-and-white as a starling—
Of those too I shall give a drove.
If he comes within my reach,
I shall present him gifts made by craftsmen;
I shall present him maidens,
Immensely beautiful, with dainty feet.
There is no equal in Great Beijing
To what Prince Kong
Has in his possession.
From the splendid yellow horses
I shall count out and drive a gift,
And from the evenly matched black horses.
I shall send word to the Kakan:
“I shall befriend Semetey
And return safely to Beijing.
I shall agree to what he said
And pay the Magnanimous One’s blood-price.
I shall say, ‘This is how matters stand,’
And depart safely for Beijing.”
So spoke Kongurbai;
Kaldais and sentries closed around him,
And to the wrathful Kalcha
Wisdom came as if from the unseen.
As its heart pounded and it pranced,
His matchless thoroughbred Black Horse—
With twelve Manchus escorting him.
Beside this uncle of yours
Stand six divisions of armed troops,
And the peerless hero Kongurbay.
The great blue-gray-bearded Manchu,
Whose jeweled button is as large as a fist—
This is how your uncle planned to deceive him.
The mediator between them was a blazing fire:
Külchoro, son of Almambet.
‘I have become Kyrgyz again after living among the Chinese;
This swine you see with your own eyes
I have made my kinsman,’ he said.
He spoke with Khan Kalcha,
Binding their promise firmly;
They swore a covenant unto death,
Exchanged many solemn words,
And licked the edge of the sword.
The cunning man, Almambet’s son,
Had drawn the line
And devised the spectacle.
The time had come for him
To begin treachery against Prince Kong.
Boundless was the resourcefulness
Of Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Who subdued the whole wide world,
A lion-warrior who took after his father.
When he was only twelve years old,
He smashed a royal camp and carried off plunder;
Hardened and sated with blood,
He was hailed as a lion cub.
He proved himself a gray wolf;
He destroyed Chynkojo
And sent that gray wolf Toltoy
Into the grave.
Yesterday he spread turmoil across many lands—
Throughout Alty-Shaar and Kokon,
As far as Margalang,
He raided and conquered them all.
Ah, a lion-warrior upheld by the saint Shay,
A bold and radiant hero—
A hero born of a noble father,
Who subdued the whole wide world.
He won Kongurbay over with his words,
Revealing what a profound champion he was;
He was about to draw the fatal line.
Such is a true hero when you behold him—
Your gray wolf was about to stage his feat.
Moving between them, that crafty man
Had marked out the city of Beijing;
He was about to bring down upon it
A calamity no mortal had ever seen.
Setting the caravan in motion and leading the migration,
He would cunningly avenge himself on your Prince Kalcha;
Such was the falcon’s intention:
To pursue him to the bitter end
And finish Kalcha by cutting off his head.
He meant to inflict surpassing torment
And avenge the noble
Prince Almambet.
If his strength sufficed, he would attack
And cast Alööke Khan’s Kongurbay
Flat upon his back.
The nimble-born lion-warrior,
A blazing fire wherever he turned,
Would make whole armies give way when he struck,
And burn every enemy he faced.
Could the valor of Almambet’s warrior son
Truly be so great?
He was both a hero and a lion,
One who subdued the whole wide world,
And they called that champion Külchoro.
Resourceful by birth, Külchoro
Displayed his cunning;
He won over the Manchu khan Ezkara
And Alööke’s Kongurbay,
Persuading Alööke with his words,
And displaying his lionhearted courage—
The warrior among spear-wielders—
He has commanding presence too,
The resourceful companion
Has strength as well.
Eloquent of tongue and masterful in speech—
Can there be another man like this companion?
Would it be right to speak so
Of that wretched companion?
Immeasurably swift,
The keen and valiant companion.
His prowess is beyond measure;
Named the companion of companions,
He has hardened himself on blood.
